beneficiile-sterilizari-cainelui-dvs-pen.title: The Health Benefits of Spaying Your Dog: A Scientific Perspective
beneficiile-sterilizari-cainelui-dvs-pen.excerpt: Spaying, or ovariohysterectomy, is a surgical procedure that involves removing a female dog's ovaries and uterus. Although it is a common practice, it is important that…
beneficiile-sterilizari-cainelui-dvs-pen.body:
Spaying, or ovariohysterectomy, is a surgical procedure that involves removing a female dog's ovaries and uterus. Although it is a common practice, it is important that you, as a pet owner, understand the significant health advantages that spaying can offer your furry friend. In this post, we will explore the scientifically supported benefits of spaying your dog, along with essential medical information.

The advantages of spaying:

1. Preventing unwanted pregnancies:

One of the most compelling reasons to spay a female dog is to prevent unwanted pregnancies. Every year, countless puppies are born to unprepared or irresponsible owners, which leads to pet overpopulation, more abandoned animals and added pressure on animal shelters. Spaying your dog helps you tackle this problem.

2. Eliminating heat cycles:

Spaying eliminates the estrous (heat) cycle in females. This cycle, characterized by hormonal fluctuations, can lead to behavioral changes and physical discomfort for both your dog and you as her owner. Spaying removes this source of stress and inconvenience.

3. Reduced risk of uterine infections:

Spaying significantly reduces the risk of uterine infections such as pyometra. This life-threatening uterine infection can cause severe abdominal pain, fever and vomiting. Pyometra is a serious condition in which the uterus becomes infected and fills with pus, requiring emergency surgery. Spaying completely prevents uterine problems from developing.

4. Lower risk of mammary gland tumors:

Research has shown that spaying before the first heat cycle greatly reduces the risk of mammary gland tumors, which are the most common type of cancer in female dogs. Spaying your dog before her first heat cycle reduces her risk of developing mammary cancer by up to 85%, and this protection decreases with each additional heat cycle. Spaying after the first heat cycle still offers significant protection. The earlier spaying is performed, the more pronounced the protective effect.

5. Lower risk of ovarian and uterine cancer:

Spaying eliminates the risk of ovarian and uterine cancer, both of which are life-threatening conditions for your female dog. These types of cancer are less common, but they can be very aggressive.

6. Preventing false pregnancies (false lactation):

Some unspayed females may experience false pregnancies (false lactation), a condition in which they show pregnancy-like symptoms without actually being pregnant. Spaying eliminates the possibility of false pregnancies (false lactation).

7. Preventing other health problems, such as:

• Uterine hemangiosarcoma: a vascular tumor of the uterus that can be fatal.
• Uterine lipomatosis: a condition that causes fatty tissue to build up in the uterus.
• Uterine prolapse: a condition in which the uterus protrudes outward through the vagina.
• Urinary tract infections: spaying can help reduce the risk of urinary tract
infections, which are more common in unspayed female dogs.

8. Behavioral benefits of spaying:

Spaying can also help improve your dog's
behavior in several ways.
• It helps prevent heat cycles and the behaviors associated with them, such as howling,
restlessness and attracting male dogs.
• It reduces the risk of aggression and territorial behavior

9. Scientific evidence supporting spaying:

Numerous studies have shown the benefits of spaying for female dogs. For example, a study published in the Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association found that spaying before the first heat cycle reduced the risk of mammary cancer by 85%. Another study, published in the Journal of Veterinary Internal Medicine, found that spaying before the first heat cycle reduced the risk of pyometra by 98%.

Timing of spaying:

The timing of spaying can influence the extent of the health benefits. Talk to your veterinarian about the best age for your dog, but it is generally recommended to have the procedure done before the first heat cycle, usually between 6 and 9 months of age. Spaying at this stage offers the most significant protection against mammary gland tumors.

Conclusion:

Spaying your dog is a responsible decision that not only prevents unwanted pregnancies but also offers a number of important health benefits. These include a reduced risk of uterine infections, mammary gland tumors and ovarian/uterine cancer. When considering spaying, talk to your veterinarian, who can give you specific recommendations based on your dog's breed, age and individual health.

Choosing to spay your dog contributes to her overall well-being and helps control the population of unwanted animals. It is an essential step toward ensuring a healthier, happier life for your beloved furry friend.

beneficiile-castrarii-caineluimascul-pen.title: The Health Benefits of Neutering Your Male Dog: A Scientific Perspective
beneficiile-castrarii-caineluimascul-pen.excerpt: Neutering is a common surgical procedure that involves removing a male dog's testicles. Although it is a standard practice, it is essential that you, as…
beneficiile-castrarii-caineluimascul-pen.body:
Neutering is a common surgical procedure that involves removing a male dog's testicles. Although it is a standard practice, it is essential that you, as a pet owner, understand the substantial health advantages that neutering can offer your furry friend. In this post, we take a closer look at the scientifically supported benefits of neutering your male dog, along with vital medical information.

The advantages of neutering:

1. Preventing unwanted matings:

One of the main reasons to neuter a male dog is to prevent unwanted litters. By reducing the chances of unplanned breeding, you can help reduce pet overpopulation and abandonment, as well as ease the pressure on animal shelters.

2. Improved behavior:

Neutering can often lead to improved behavior in male dogs. It can help reduce aggressive tendencies, roaming and dominance-related problems. These behaviors can lead to dogs being hit by cars, getting lost or being exposed to various diseases.

3. Preventing testicular tumors:

Neutering eliminates the risk of testicular tumors, which are the second most common type of cancer in male dogs. These tumors can be aggressive, but neutering significantly reduces their occurrence.

4. Reduced risk of prostate problems:

Neutering can reduce the risk of benign prostatic hyperplasia (enlarged prostate), prostatitis (inflammation of the prostate) and even prostate cancer. These conditions can be painful and life-threatening. Neutering reduces the risk of prostate cancer by up to 70%.

5. Preventing perianal tumors:

Perianal tumors, which are growths located near the dog's anus, are rare in neutered males. These tumors can be difficult to manage and may require surgery. Neutering reduces the risk of them developing by up to 80%.

6. Less territory marking:

Intact male dogs are more likely to mark their territory by urinating on various objects. Neutering can help reduce or eliminate this behavior.

7. Training becomes easier:

Neutered dogs are often more focused and obedient, which makes them easier to train, as they are not as distracted by various stimuli.

8. Aggression:

Intact male dogs are more likely to be aggressive toward other dogs and people. This can make them difficult to handle and can lead to biting incidents.

Scientific evidence supporting neutering:

Numerous studies have shown the benefits of neutering for male dogs. For example, a study published in the Journal of Veterinary Internal Medicine found that neutering before six months of age reduces the risk of testicular cancer by 100%. Another study, published in the Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association, found that neutering reduces the risk of prostate cancer by up to 70%.

Timing of neutering:

The optimal age for neutering varies by breed and by individual dog, so it is best to consult your veterinarian. In general, neutering can be performed from as early as 6 months of age, although some veterinarians recommend waiting a little longer for large or giant breeds to allow full skeletal development. Your veterinarian will guide you according to your dog's specific needs.

Conclusion:

Neutering your male dog is a responsible decision that offers a number of health benefits, including the prevention of testicular tumors, prostate problems and perianal tumors. In addition, it can help ease certain behavioral problems, making life more harmonious for both you and your dog.

By neutering your male dog, you contribute to his overall well-being and play a part in reducing the number of homeless animals. It is a thoughtful step toward ensuring a healthier, happier life for your beloved furry friend. If you are planning to have your dog neutered, talk to your veterinarian to determine the best timing and approach for your dog's specific needs.

un-ghid-cuprinzator-pentru-ingrijirea-pi.title: A Comprehensive Guide to Cat Care: Keep Your Feline Friend Happy and Healthy
un-ghid-cuprinzator-pentru-ingrijirea-pi.excerpt: Cats are wonderful companions, and caring for them means giving them the best possible love, attention and medical care. As a cat owner, you play a…
un-ghid-cuprinzator-pentru-ingrijirea-pi.body:
Cats are wonderful companions, and caring for them means giving them the best possible love, attention and medical care. As a cat owner, you play a crucial role in making sure your feline friend lives a healthy and happy life. In this comprehensive guide, we will explore the essential aspects of cat care to help you be the best cat parent you can be.

1. A nutritious diet: the foundation of feline health

Proper nutrition is the cornerstone of your cat's well-being. Cats are obligate carnivores, which means their diet should consist mainly of high-quality animal protein.

Commercial cat food: choose a complete and nutritionally balanced cat food, either dry or canned, that meets your cat's specific needs. Ask your veterinarian for recommendations.

Fresh water: always give your cat fresh, clean water to keep it hydrated and to support its overall health. Avoid harmful foods: never feed your cat chocolate, alcohol, onions, garlic, grapes, raisins or any other food that is toxic to cats

2. Regular veterinary check-ups: keep an eye on health

Regular visits to the veterinarian are vital for your cat's health and longevity. Veterinarians can offer advice on diet, behavior and medical issues.

Vaccinations: follow the vaccination schedule recommended by your veterinarian to protect your cat from common diseases. Parasite control: give preventive treatments against fleas, ticks, worms and other parasites, as prescribed by your veterinarian.

Health monitoring: regular check-ups help monitor your cat's health and detect any problems early.

3. Grooming and hygiene: keep your cat fresh and clean

Regular grooming and good hygiene are essential for your cat's health and happiness. Brushing: depending on the breed, regular brushing helps reduce shedding and prevents hairballs. Nail trimming: keep your cat's nails trimmed to a suitable length to prevent discomfort or potential injuries.

Dental care: brush your cat's teeth regularly and ask your veterinarian for dental health advice.

4. Provide a stimulating environment: mental and physical enrichment

Cats need both mental and physical stimulation to stay happy and healthy. Interactive toys: offer a variety of toys to keep your cat engaged and entertained. Toys that mimic prey can be especially appealing. Climbing structures: cats love to climb and perch. Give them cat trees or shelves to explore and rest on.

Interactive playtime: regular play sessions with toys such as feather wands or laser pointers keep your cat active and mentally stimulated.

5. Create a safe living space: ensuring safety and comfort

A safe and comfortable environment is essential for your cat's well-being.

Litter box: keep the litter box clean and in a quiet, accessible location. Comfortable resting places: provide cozy beds and safe resting areas where your cat can relax.

Safe windows and balconies: make sure all windows and balconies are secure to prevent accidents.

6. Unconditional love and attention: building a strong bond

Your cat needs love, attention and affection to thrive and be happy. Spend quality time together: set aside time every day to cuddle, play and interact with your cat. Cats appreciate companionship.

Positive reinforcement: use treats and praise to reinforce good behavior and strengthen your bond with your cat. By following these fundamental principles of cat care, you can provide a loving and nurturing environment for your feline companion. Remember, a happy and healthy cat is a joy to have and enriches your life in countless ways.

primul-caine-aici-ai-cateva-sfaturi-pent.title: Your First Dog? Here Are a Few Tips for a Happy, Healthy Dog!
primul-caine-aici-ai-cateva-sfaturi-pent.excerpt: If you've just bought a dog and aren't sure exactly what to do, we've put together a few steps for you to follow below: Make sure your puppy is dewormed from 2 weeks of age…
primul-caine-aici-ai-cateva-sfaturi-pent.body:
If you've just bought a dog and aren't sure exactly what to do, we've put together a few steps for you to follow below:

Make sure your puppy is dewormed from 2 weeks of age under the guidance of your veterinarian; you can consult a veterinarian about this here.

For the first 6 weeks, don't let your puppy near other dogs or in places where other dogs have been. This substantially reduces the risk of infection with canine parvovirus, which is very dangerous. To make sure you are up to date with vaccinations, you can find out more here.

In its first months of life, you should feed your puppy quality food, ideally a Puppy/Starter formula; you can find more information here.

You can also add some dietary supplements for healthy bones and joints and proper growth, especially in the first months of life, on your veterinarian's recommendation.

Don't overdo the treats.

Don't give it food from your plate (milk, bones, fat); it needs to understand that its food is different from yours.

Don't give it bones: they will make it constipated, can perforate its intestines and can cause an intestinal blockage, all of which require emergency surgery.

Don't give it chocolate: it is toxic to dogs, disrupts their metabolism, raises their blood pressure and overstimulates their nervous system, with a high risk of death.

Don't let it eat grapes or raisins: they can cause serious kidney damage.

Don't give it sweets: sugar makes it hyperactive and can lead to diabetes and obesity, and xylitol is highly toxic to dogs.

Avoid giving it vitamins meant for humans and, above all, never let it try alcohol, which is toxic to dogs.

Avoid onions and garlic, as they cause anemia; bread in small amounts won't harm it, but it has no nutritional value. Don't give it milk to drink, as dogs are lactose intolerant; small amounts of yogurt, however, won't harm it.

If you feel sorry for it, and it's surely a little glutton, you can share some food from your plate: boiled eggs, ham, boneless fish, carrots, peas, cheese, banana or potatoes, but only in moderate amounts.

Avoid frequent baths in the first 3 months of life: no more than once a month, using a shampoo recommended by your veterinarian

Keep up with vaccinations and regular parasite treatments, which are essential especially in the first months of life, when your puppy is most vulnerable.

Try to teach it basic commands (sit, down, come, back, no, etc.)

Choose a skilled veterinarian.

Give it attention, love and respect, and it will love you unconditionally.

Be prepared for possible changes in its behavior and health.

Don't forget that it will be your best friend, and you need to take good care of it.

Also consider a health care plan for your dog; you can find more information about our available subscription plans right here.

d7cdeee4f897.question: What type of food should I give my dog or cat?
d7cdeee4f897.answer:
There are different types of pet food, such as dry food, wet food and even grain-free food. Our veterinarians can help you choose food tailored to your dog's or cat's needs.

Different foods offer various health benefits, from supporting dental health to managing weight gain. Your veterinarian can also make suggestions based on your pet's age, breed, reproductive status and lifestyle, as nutritional needs change throughout your pet's life.

You can find out more about our nutrition services here.

a269afa3f289.question: Why does my dog eat grass?
a269afa3f289.answer:
Dogs eat grass to meet dietary needs or to soothe themselves when they feel unwell. Usually, you don't need to worry about your pet coming to any harm from eating grass, but as a good pet owner, you will want to ask yourself “why” if you see it doing so! Perhaps its current diet isn't giving it the nutrients it needs, so it is trying to meet those needs with the grass it eats.

Also, a dog that feels something is wrong with its stomach may find a quick natural remedy by eating grass. However, if your pet suddenly starts eating large amounts of grass, experts recommend taking it to a veterinarian for an evaluation, as this behavior may well mean that something is seriously wrong and it is trying to help itself.

You can find out more about our nutrition services here.

ddf63f842ca3.question: My older dog seems to have dementia. Is that possible?
ddf63f842ca3.answer:
According to some studies, 50% of dogs over 11 years of age show signs of cognitive decline (which some might classify as dementia). So the answer to your question is YES: an older dog can suffer from cognitive decline/dementia.

If your dog shows some of the symptoms listed below, you may want to bring this to the veterinarian's attention during the consultation, so that our veterinarians can test for cognitive dysfunction syndrome.

Seems lethargic

Is no longer interested in its usual activities

Gets stuck on certain things/objects around it

Is disoriented

No longer recognizes animals or people it knew well

Seems confused

Is extremely irritable

Canine cognitive dysfunction syndrome cannot be cured, but its symptoms can be treated. Our dogs grow old, and when that happens, they no longer seem able to behave the way they did when they were young. However, there are a few things you can do to help your pet in this situation. Once there is a diagnosis, you as the owner can choose either to give your pet the medication needed to help slow the decline, or to opt for therapy options, which you can discuss with one of our veterinarians. Both options, especially when used together, can be of great help to your friend.

You can find out more about our laboratory testing services by clicking here.

d2bbcec1e10f.question: Should I brush my dog's/cat's teeth?
d2bbcec1e10f.answer:
The answer to this question is YES, absolutely! It is very important to brush your pet's teeth regularly, using, of course, a toothbrush and toothpaste made for pets! You may want to know why cleaning their teeth is so important. Below are a few reasons to help you better understand why your pet needs regular tooth brushing.

Signs of tooth and gum disease begin to appear in 80% of dogs after the age of 3. Cats also face the risk of developing dental disease, the most common being periodontal disease.

For these reasons, veterinarians recommend an annual professional cleaning (scaling), especially as your pet gets older, as well as daily brushing by pet owners to prevent dental problems.

The serious effects of dental problems can be prevented through proactive preventive care. Help your pet keep its beautiful smile; by doing so, you will promote good overall health!

You can find out more about our dental scaling services by clicking here.

8c8e7e4e09e0.question: What happens during a general check-up for my pet?
8c8e7e4e09e0.answer:
At a routine veterinary exam, the veterinarian will perform a thorough physical examination of your pet to check its overall health and well-being. The veterinarian will weigh your pet and take its temperature to check for any signs of fever or changes in weight. The veterinarian will perform a physical exam of your pet, checking its eyes, ears, nose, mouth, teeth, skin, coat, joints and overall body condition. The veterinarian will listen to your pet's heart and lungs to check for any abnormalities. The veterinarian will palpate your pet's abdomen to check for any signs of pain, lumps or abnormal masses.

The veterinarian may give your pet any vaccines it needs to protect it from common diseases. The veterinarian may check your pet for external parasites, such as fleas and ticks, and may recommend medication to prevent or treat them.

The veterinarian may recommend blood tests to check for any underlying health problems. The veterinarian will examine your pet's teeth and gums to check for any signs of dental disease. The veterinarian may ask you about your pet's behavior and give you advice on how to resolve any behavioral problems. During the exam, the veterinarian can also discuss any concerns you have about your pet's health, diet or behavior and offer recommendations for preventive care or treatment.

You can view our home consultation services by clicking here.

395581c1718b.question: When should I have my dog or cat spayed or neutered?
395581c1718b.answer:
It is usually recommended that females be spayed and males neutered between six months and one year of age. Sometimes, however, exceptions are made depending on age, breed, weight and health status (for example, a puppy that is too small should not be put under anesthesia until it is bigger). Your veterinarian will let you know when the time is right to spay or neuter your pet.

You can find out more about our surgery services by clicking here.

e3a388dacccc.question: When does my dog need blood tests?
e3a388dacccc.answer:
Veterinarians recommend annual blood tests starting at around 7 years of age, which is considered the beginning of the “senior” years. All dogs and cats should have a set of blood tests before general anesthesia, if possible.

Blood tests help determine several things, such as whether a pet's red and white blood cell counts are normal, whether the liver, kidneys, pancreas and other internal organs appear to be working well/normally, and whether electrolyte balance and hydration status are normal.

You can find out more about our laboratory testing services by clicking here.

42e9a97e816a.question: What if I find lumps on or under my pet's skin?
42e9a97e816a.answer:
Dogs and cats can develop growths and masses on the surface of the skin or under it. This is quite common in dogs, and there is a wide variety of malignant (cancerous) as well as benign (non-cancerous) growths and masses.

Because there are so many types, and cancer is “the great imitator” and can look like anything, it is always a good idea to have every lump evaluated by your veterinarian. A fine-needle aspirate (using a needle to collect cells from the mass) and cytology (examining the cells under a microscope using special stains) can help with diagnosis, but sometimes a surgical biopsy or complete removal of the mass is needed to diagnose it.

You can view our dermatology services here.

95ecc9b15907.question: How often should I bathe my dog/cat?
95ecc9b15907.answer:
In general, cats don't need to be bathed because they groom themselves. Most dogs shouldn't be bathed more often than every 2-3 weeks, because bathing them more often may strip away some of their skin's protective oils. This can of course change if, for example, your pet has a particular skin condition, so at a routine check-up your veterinarian can tell whether your pet has special circumstances, allergies or a skin infection and needs to be bathed more often.

You can view our dermatology services here.

96d2cf77fe40.question: What are the most common diseases I should watch out for in my dog/cat?
96d2cf77fe40.answer:
The most common diseases seen in dogs and cats are dental disease, skin infections, ear infections and cancerous/non-cancerous skin masses. Annual exams, open communication with your veterinarian and regular tests can help keep these and other diseases from becoming severe and help your furry friend live a longer, happier life.

You can find out more about our internal medicine services by clicking here.

af50028d32fc.question: How often should my pet exercise?
af50028d32fc.answer: Dogs and cats should exercise every day, just like people. It is important to keep their joints and muscles moving, to maintain a healthy weight and body condition, and to keep pets stimulated and entertained so they don't become overweight, bored and possibly destructive.

3ace4f15f51f.question: What are the best parasite treatments for my pet?
3ace4f15f51f.answer:
There are many types of parasites that can cause health problems for your pet, and some can even cause health problems for you. Some parasites live in your pet's blood vessels and heart (heartworms), others live in your pet's intestines (roundworms, whipworms, hookworms, tapeworms), some live at least part of their life on your pet's body (fleas, ticks), some bite pets for a blood meal (mosquitoes), and others like to live in their ears (mites). These are just a few examples.

There are many medications for parasite prevention. It is best to ask your veterinarian which medication is right for your pet. “Dr Google” can lead you down the wrong path, and you may end up with treatments that don't work or, even worse, that can do your pet more harm.

Some treatments will also be needed for your home environment, for example against fleas, because fleas stay on your pet to take a blood meal and then drop off to complete their reproductive cycle elsewhere, such as in carpets or the pens where pets spend their time.
